summary: Summarizes documents from the IETF and the ITU-T that relate to accounting, meaning the recording of how network resources are used. It is an informational survey.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a reading list of how different groups keep track of who used how much of a network.

subtitle: Survey of attributes and formats for recording how network resources are used

tldr.problem: Network operators need to record how users and services consume network resources, but different organizations and protocols define accounting attributes and record formats in inconsistent ways.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys accounting approaches in IETF protocols (RADIUS, DIAMETER, RTFM, ISDN MIB, AToM MIB, QoS) and ITU-T standards (Q.825), classifies their attributes, and discusses record format options and service definition challenges.
tldr.outcome: The document identifies requirements for a well-defined set of accounting attributes and a simple interchange format, highlighting the need for extensibility, versioning support, and service definition independence.

facts.value: Service definition, extensibility, versioning, transport, attributes

today: RFC 2924 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. The accounting challenges and requirements it identifies remain relevant to network management, billing, and service measurement systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2924 is an informational survey of documents from the IETF and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T) that relate to accounting, the recording of network resource usage. Accounting differs from authentication (proving who you are) and authorization (what you are allowed to do); instead, it focuses on measuring and reporting what users actually consumed: bandwidth, connection time, memory usage, and other metrics.

The RFC notes that many existing accounting formats and protocols suffer from limited extensibility and lack of support for versioning or multiple service types. Different standards (such as RADIUS for dial-in accounting, Q.825 for call detail recording, and RTFM for traffic flow measurement) each define their own attributes and record formats, making it difficult to integrate accounting systems across organizations.

The document presents a classification scheme for accounting attributes and examines the advantages and disadvantages of different record format options and transport methods. It discusses fundamental challenges such as service definition independence, extensibility, and versioning that any unified accounting framework must address.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how different parts of the internet write down what you used, and points out that nobody agrees on exactly what to write or how to write it.

sections.title: Architecture and Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC establishes a common architecture and vocabulary. Service Elements provide services to Service Consumers and report Usage Events to Accounting Servers. A Usage Event describes one instance of service usage and is composed of Usage Attributes (measurable metrics such as duration, bytes transferred, or service type).

A Service Definition specifies a particular service and includes a name or identifier, versioning information, and a collection of Properties. An Attribute-Value Pair (AVP) is the basic representation of a single usage attribute and its value. This terminology unifies how different standards discuss similar concepts, though they may use different names.

In a typical accounting architecture, a Service Element generates Usage Events before, during, or after providing a service and sends them singly or in bulk to an Accounting Server. The Accounting Server forwards Usage Events to other systems, possibly in different administrative domains. The challenge is that different services (voice calls, data sessions, video streaming, bandwidth reservations) have different attributes that need to be recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone using a service creates records about what they used. These records list details like how long they used it, how much data went through, and what kind of service it was. Different services track different details.

sections.title: Standards and Protocols Surveyed
sections.content:
The document surveys accounting in multiple IETF working groups. RADIUS is a widely-used protocol for authentication and accounting in dial-in networks that carries attributes in Type-Length-Value (TLV) triples; RADIUS Accounting Attributes track session identifiers, input and output octets, session time, and termination reasons. DIAMETER is a proposed successor to RADIUS with similar concepts but improvements.

RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement) is a framework for measuring network traffic and includes detailed accounting attributes in ASN.1 format. The ISDN MIB defines accounting attributes for ISDN connections. AToM MIB covers accounting for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks. For Quality of Service, RSVP and DIFFSERV define their own accounting attributes related to bandwidth and service levels.

The ITU-T standard Q.825 (Call Detail Recording) defines call accounting for voice networks with attributes such as called number, calling number, start time, duration, and cost. The document notes that no unified scheme exists; each protocol or service defines attributes independently, creating management challenges when systems from different vendors or working groups must interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone systems, data networks, voice networks, and internet services all track what people used, but each one writes down different information in different ways. This part of the document lists what each system tracks.

sections.title: Record Formats and Transport Methods
sections.content:
The RFC examines three main categories of accounting record formats. ASN.1 Records (used by RTFM and AToM MIB) use formal syntax that is extensible and machine-parseable. Binary Records (RADIUS and DIAMETER) use compact representations with fixed headers and variable-length attribute fields, making them efficient for transmission. Text Records (such as ROAMOPS formats) are human-readable and easier to debug.

The RFC discusses the trade-off between integrated and separate record formats and transport protocols. Some systems combine authentication, authorization, and accounting in one protocol (like RADIUS); others separate them. Integrated approaches simplify deployment but may be less flexible for future changes. Separate approaches allow optimization for each function but require coordination between systems.

Transport methods vary from UDP-based protocols (RADIUS, DIAMETER) suitable for low-latency requirements to file-based transfer and bulk reporting. The document notes that record format and protocol design are distinct choices, and that different services may benefit from different transport approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: The actual records can be written in different ways: special computer format, packed binary form, or plain text. Each way has good and bad points depending on whether you care more about size, speed, or being able to read it.

sections.title: Service Definitions and Extensibility
sections.content:
A key challenge identified in the RFC is service definition independence. Current accounting systems are often built for specific service types (dial-in, voice calls, QoS sessions) and do not easily extend to new services. The framework should allow service definitions to be independent of the transport protocol and allow new service types to be added without redesigning the core system.

Versioning is another critical requirement. As services evolve, new attributes must be added and old attributes may be deprecated. Accounting systems must be able to handle multiple versions of a service definition and migrate gracefully when protocols are updated. Systems must also support compound service definitions, where a single service comprises multiple service sub-types (for example, a multimedia session combining voice and video).

The RFC emphasizes the need for tagged, typed data with standard type definitions, allowing any system to identify and interpret accounting data even if the service was defined elsewhere. Transaction identifiers must uniquely identify related accounting events (such as all records belonging to one billing transaction). These requirements point toward a future unified accounting framework that can handle diverse services across multiple administrative domains.
sections.plainLanguage: As new services are invented, the accounting system has to handle them without breaking the old ones. Different organizations might define the same service differently, and old software needs to understand new services. The challenge is making the system flexible enough for all that.
